title: Lady Be Good: The Bomber Found in the Sahara 15 Years After It Vanished

opener.caption: The wreck in the Libyan desert

scenes.label: LIBYAN DESERT, 5 APRIL 1943
lines: Two o'clock in the morning, April 5th, 1943. Over the Libyan desert, an American bomber is running out of fuel.
Nine young airmen jump out into the dark.
They believe they are close to the Mediterranean coast, and close to home.
In fact, they are far out over the desert, hundreds of miles south of their base.
Their plane, the Lady Be Good, flies on without them.

scenes.sub: The bomber the desert kept for fifteen years
lines: For fifteen years, nobody knew where she had gone.
When she was found, she was almost perfectly preserved. But her crew was not aboard.

scenes.title: Spring 1943
lines: The Lady Be Good was a B-24D Liberator of the 514th Bomb Squadron, 376th Bomb Group, flying from Soluch, near Benghazi in Libya.
Her crew had arrived in Libya on March 18th, 1943. The raid of April 4th, on Naples harbour, was their first combat mission.
Twenty-five B-24s took part. The Lady Be Good flew in the second wave, and turned back before reaching the target.
That night, twenty-four bombers came home. She did not.

scenes.title: Nine men
lines: The pilot was First Lieutenant William Hatton. His co-pilot was Robert Toner, and the navigator was D. P. Hays.
With them flew bombardier John Woravka, engineer Harold Ripslinger, radio operator Robert LaMotte, and gunners Guy Shelley, Vernon Moore and Samuel Adams.
Nine men, on their first mission.

scenes.label: OVER SOLUCH, NIGHT
lines: Coming home in the dark, the bomber flew right over its own base. Flares were fired. Nobody aboard saw them.
The base's radio direction finder gave them a bearing that seemed to say they were still on course for home.
But that equipment could not tell whether a plane was flying toward the base or away from it. The bearing looked the same.

scenes.label: SOUTH, INTO THE DESERT
lines: So instead of approaching the coast, they were flying south, deeper and deeper into the desert.
Toner's diary suggests they never realised they had crossed the coast. They thought they were still about a hundred miles from base.
At about two in the morning, out of fuel, they jumped.

scenes.note: About 400 to 440 miles into the desert
lines: Without a crew, the Lady Be Good flew on for about sixteen miles.
She came down on her belly, skidded nearly seven hundred yards, and broke in two behind the wings.
There she lay, roughly four hundred miles south of her base.
On November 9th, 1958, a British Petroleum oil exploration team spotted the wreck from the air.
In early 1959, a team reached her on the ground.
She was astonishingly well preserved. A machine gun fired when its trigger was pulled. The radio still worked.
There was water aboard, and a thermos of tea that was still drinkable.
But there were no bodies, and no sign of the crew. In March 1960, Life magazine told her story to America.

scenes.title: Looking for nine men
lines: From May to August 1959, Captain Myron Fuller and anthropologist Wesley Neep searched the area.
They found parachutes and flight boots laid out as arrows, pointing north. A trail left by the crew. But no remains.
Then, on February 11th, 1960, oil workers found five of the men together on a plateau, about eighty miles from the wreck.
Hatton, Toner, Hays, LaMotte and Adams.
With them was co-pilot Robert Toner's diary.

scenes.title: Robert Toner's diary
lines: The first entry tells the story in one breath. Out of gas, jumped, landed in the desert at two in the morning. No one badly hurt. Can't find John.
John was Woravka, the bombardier. His parachute had not opened properly. He was found in August 1960, about twelve miles from the wreck.
The others started walking north-west, with a few rations and half a canteen of water.
April 7th. Everyone getting weak, can't get very far, prayers all the time.

scenes.label: CALANSCIO SAND SEA
lines: On April 9th, Shelley, Ripslinger and Moore went on ahead, to try to bring help.
The others waited, and grew weaker. The last entry is dated Monday, April 12th, 1943.
Experts had expected men in that heat to walk perhaps twenty-five or thirty miles, and to live about two days.
They lasted eight days, on almost no water, in midday heat up to about one hundred and thirty degrees Fahrenheit.

scenes.title: How far they got
lines: In May 1960, a larger search, Operation Climax, set out with nineteen men, six vehicles and two helicopters.
On May 12th, they found Guy Shelley, more than twenty miles beyond the others.
Days later, a helicopter crew spotted Harold Ripslinger on the slope of a dune, even further on. By one count, he had walked about a hundred and nine miles.
Shelley and Ripslinger had kept diaries too.
Vernon Moore has never been found, despite a search of about six thousand three hundred square miles.

scenes.label: THE LEGEND
lines: Parts of the bomber were taken away and fitted to other aircraft. A legend grew that they were cursed.
A transport plane carrying her radio receiver ditched in the Mediterranean. Another aircraft, carrying one of her armrests, crashed in the Gulf of Sidra.
That's a legend, not proof of anything. But it became part of her story.
A stained-glass window for the crew, first dedicated in Libya in 1961, now hangs at the National Museum of the US Air Force.
In 1994, a Libyan team recovered what was left of the wreck. It is now stored at a Libyan air base.

scenes.label: LIBYAN DESERT
lines: Nine men, on their first mission, lost because of a radio bearing that pointed both ways.
Eight of them have been found. One is still out there, somewhere in the sand.
If they had known where the plane came down, could they have survived? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for a new true mystery every day.

youtube.title: Lady Be Good: The Bomber Found in the Sahara 15 Years After It Vanished
youtube.description:
On 4 April 1943, the B-24D 'Lady Be Good' of the 376th Bomb Group flew its crew's first mission, a raid on Naples, and never returned to its base at Soluch, Libya. In the dark it overflew the base; its single-loop radio direction finder could not show whether the plane was inbound or outbound, and the crew flew deep into the Libyan desert before bailing out at about 2 a.m. on 5 April. The plane was spotted by a BP oil exploration team on 9 November 1958, remarkably intact. In 1960, eight of the nine crew were found, along with co-pilot Robert Toner's diary; Vernon Moore has never been found. Distances walked differ between sources; we give approximate figures.

Scenes marked RECONSTRUCTION are illustrated dramatizations based on historical accounts. Opening photo from Wikimedia Commons (credit below); all other visuals are original illustrations, except photo scenes credited on screen.
